questions.q: Why does ShiftCode belong on a new dw.DimShift dimension rather than as a raw column added directly to dw.FactWorkOrder?
options: It's a low-cardinality descriptive attribute, the same shape as ScrapReason — modeling it as a dimension avoids duplicating descriptive text and lets a later rename (e.g. "Day" to "First Shift") update one dimension row instead of every historical fact row
SQL Server does not allow adding new columns to an existing fact table
SSIS cannot map a new source column into an existing staging table
Fact tables are only allowed to contain foreign keys, never any other column type
questions.explain: ShiftCode is a small set of fixed, descriptive values describing a characteristic of the work order — exactly the shape ScrapReason already took as dw.DimScrapReason, so it gets modeled the same way.

questions.q: Put the five-stop ripple in the order this lesson describes it: staging, SSIS mapping, warehouse, SSRS, Power BI. Why does this order matter?
options: Each stop only works because the one before it already landed — an SSIS mapping added before the staging column exists fails, and a report parameter added before the warehouse column exists just produces blanks
The order doesn't matter; all five can be changed in any sequence with identical results
SSRS and Power BI must be updated before the warehouse, since they are the tools business users actually see
The staging table is optional and can be skipped entirely for an additive change
questions.explain: Each stage depends on the previous one already existing — you can't map a column that isn't in staging yet, and a report can't show a warehouse column that doesn't exist yet.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe the staging and warehouse changes as "additive," and why does that matter?
options: They add new nullable columns and a new dimension without altering any existing column's type or meaning, so every report and dashboard already in production keeps working unmodified
Additive means the change can only ever add rows, never columns
Additive changes always require every consuming report to be rebuilt from scratch immediately
Additive changes are only possible in Power BI, never in SQL Server or SSRS
questions.explain: Because nothing that already existed changed shape or meaning, WorkOrderProductionSummary.rdl and the Power BI dashboard keep working exactly as they did before, with no forced same-day update.

questions.q: What should ShiftKey be, on dw.FactWorkOrder rows loaded before the ShiftCode change was made?
options: NULL (or a resolved "Unknown Shift" member) — a normal, expected state for a Type 0 dimension backfilled after the fact
An error value that must be manually corrected before any report can run
Automatically set to the most common shift code across all historical rows
Impossible — historical rows must be deleted and reloaded before this change can be made at all
questions.explain: Pre-change historical rows legitimately have no shift recorded; NULL (or an Unknown Shift member) is the expected, correct state, not a data quality failure.

questions.q: After making this schema change, what does this lesson say to do with Lesson 10's validation checklist?
options: Re-run all four checks exactly as written, plus one addition: confirm ShiftKey resolves to a real DimShift row or is legitimately NULL for pre-change rows
Discard it entirely and design a completely new set of checks specific to shifts
Skip validation this time, since the change is additive and therefore assumed safe
Only re-run the checks against the Power BI dashboard, since SSRS wasn't changed in this scenario
questions.explain: The same row-count, orphaned-key, and cross-tool checks still apply after any change — this one just adds a ShiftKey orphan check on top of them.
